description: Medical knowledge base for skin lesion analysis - Educational purposes only
disclaimer: This information is for educational purposes only and should not be used for medical diagnosis. Always consult a qualified healthcare professional.

commonTypes.name: Seborrheic Keratosis
commonTypes.description: Common non-cancerous skin growth that appears as a brown, black, or tan growth with a waxy, scaly, slightly elevated appearance

commonTypes.name: Dermatofibroma
commonTypes.description: Small, firm bump that often appears on the legs, typically brownish in color

commonTypes.name: Common Nevus (Mole)
commonTypes.description: Benign growth of melanocytes that appears as a small, dark spot on the skin

generalCharacteristics.asymmetry: Symmetrical appearance when divided in half
generalCharacteristics.color: Uniform color throughout, typically one shade
generalCharacteristics.diameter: Usually stable in size, often less than 6mm
generalCharacteristics.evolution: Minimal or no changes over time

recommendations: Monitor for any changes in size, color, or shape
Protect skin from excessive sun exposure
Document with photos for future comparison

commonTypes.name: Atypical Nevus (Dysplastic Nevus)
commonTypes.description: Unusual-looking mole that may have irregular features but is not yet cancerous
commonTypes.prevalence: 5-10% of adults have at least one

commonTypes.name: Actinic Keratosis
commonTypes.description: Rough, scaly patch caused by sun damage that could potentially develop into skin cancer
commonTypes.prevalence: Very common in fair-skinned individuals over 40
commonTypes.riskLevel: Precancerous, 5-10% may progress to squamous cell carcinoma

commonTypes.name: Changing Lesion
commonTypes.description: Any skin lesion showing changes in the ABCDE criteria

warningSignsABCDE.A: Asymmetry - One half doesn't match the other half
warningSignsABCDE.B: Border irregularity - Edges are ragged, notched, or blurred
warningSignsABCDE.C: Color variation - Multiple colors or uneven distribution
warningSignsABCDE.E: Evolution - Changes in size, shape, color, or symptoms

recommendations: Avoid further sun exposure to the area
Do not attempt to remove or treat at home
Document with clear photos from multiple angles
Note any symptoms: itching, bleeding, or pain
Bring list of any changes you've observed

commonTypes.name: Melanoma
commonTypes.description: Most serious type of skin cancer that develops in melanocytes
commonTypes.prevalence: 1 in 27 men and 1 in 40 women will develop melanoma
commonTypes.riskLevel: High risk, can spread to other organs if untreated

commonTypes.name: Basal Cell Carcinoma
commonTypes.description: Most common form of skin cancer, appears as a pearly or waxy bump
commonTypes.riskLevel: Rarely spreads but can be locally destructive

commonTypes.name: Squamous Cell Carcinoma
commonTypes.description: Second most common skin cancer, appears as a firm red nodule or flat lesion
commonTypes.riskLevel: Can spread if untreated, requires prompt treatment

criticalFeatures.appearance: Highly irregular borders, multiple colors, asymmetrical
criticalFeatures.texture: May be raised, ulcerated, or bleeding
criticalFeatures.symptoms: May itch, hurt, or bleed spontaneously
criticalFeatures.growth: Rapid or noticeable changes in size or appearance

urgentRecommendations: Request urgent evaluation if rapidly changing
Prepare medical history including sun exposure and family history
Document all symptoms and timeline of changes
Do not delay - early detection significantly improves outcomes
Consider seeking second opinion if diagnosis unclear

environmental: Excessive UV exposure from sun or tanning beds
History of severe sunburns, especially in childhood
Living in high-altitude or sunny climates
genetic: Fair skin, light hair, and light eyes
Family history of melanoma or skin cancer
medical: Certain medications that increase sun sensitivity

sunProtection: Reapply sunscreen every 2 hours when outdoors
Seek shade during peak sun hours (10am-4pm)
Wear protective clothing, wide-brimmed hats, and UV-blocking sunglasses
selfExamination: Check entire body including scalp, between toes, and back
Use mirrors or ask partner to check hard-to-see areas
Follow the ABCDE rule for mole evaluation
professionalCare: Annual full-body skin exam by dermatologist
More frequent exams if high-risk factors present
Immediate evaluation of any changing or concerning lesions
Keep records of all skin examinations and biopsies
